topic.topic: Why a lunar month lasts longer than the Moon’s orbit
topic.angle: Explain the difference between the Moon’s roughly 27.3-day orbit around Earth and the roughly 29.5 days between matching phases, using the Moon’s and Earth’s simultaneous motion around the Sun to make the distinction intuitive.

decisions.reason: A clear, evergreen question supported by NASA’s explanation of orbital and phase cycles; it avoids the archived daytime-Moon and eclipse topics.
NASA’s Moon Phases page supports the 27.3-day orbit, 29.5-day phase cycle, and the role of Earth’s motion around the Sun; the topic is ready to draft.
The NASA phases source supports the cycle lengths and phase descriptions; an independent factual review should verify the moving-Earth explanation and whether any claims need tighter wording.
feedback: Paragraph 2’s central explanation—that Earth and the Moon travel around the Sun together, shifting the Sun’s direction relative to them and leaving the Moon short of its previous Sun-Earth alignment after one orbit—is not established by the supplied source.

Paragraph 4 says the Moon must continue around its orbit to “catch up” with a changing alignment. The supplied source gives the orbital and phase-cycle durations but does not explain the difference through this catch-up mechanism, so that causal assertion is unsupported.

decisions.reason: The phase lengths and illumination are supported, but the causal explanation needs evidence. NASA’s already-retrieved Moon Facts page notes Earth’s motion and that the Moon appears to orbit from our perspective every 29 days; use it alongside the phases page and avoid unsupported catch-up wording.

The current draft still lacks a supported explanation of how Earth’s motion relates the two periods. NASA’s retrieved pages support the orbital and phase-cycle lengths and note that Earth’s motion affects the Moon’s apparent cycle.
